articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 million question: Where the tourism tax dollars actually go
articles.dek: Bed tax collections hit record highs last fiscal year. A Flightline review of spending records shows the gap between what the Tourist Development Council promises and what it delivers.
brief: Escambia County collected $47.3 million in tourist development taxes in FY 2025, a 12% increase over the previous year
The Flightline's review of TDC expenditures found $8.2 million in marketing contracts with limited performance metrics and $3.1 million in administrative costs that have grown faster than collections
Beach renourishment—the stated priority—received 23% of total spending while out-of-market advertising campaigns took 41%
articles.body:
The conference room on the third floor of the Escambia County Central Office Complex seats maybe forty people. On the second Tuesday of each month, rarely more than a dozen show up. Most are hoteliers. A few are county staff. Almost never is there anyone from the public.

This is where $47.3 million gets divvied up.

The Tourist Development Council meets here to recommend how Escambia County should spend its bed tax—the 5% surcharge visitors pay on hotel and short-term rental stays. The money, by state law, must promote tourism. What that means in practice is the subject of considerable interpretation.

The Flightline spent three months reviewing TDC expenditure reports, marketing contracts, meeting minutes, and state tourism data. What emerged is a portrait of a quasi-governmental body that operates with minimal oversight, measures success by metrics it largely controls, and consistently prioritizes out-of-state advertising over the beach infrastructure its own strategic plan calls essential.

The money flow

Escambia County's tourist development tax collections have grown 67% since fiscal year 2019. Last year's $47.3 million was a record. The county now collects more in bed taxes than it does in gas taxes, building permit fees, and franchise fees combined.

Where does it go?

The largest single category is marketing—$19.4 million, or 41% of total expenditures. This includes contracts with two advertising agencies, Visit Pensacola's operational budget, and a $2.8 million digital advertising buy that runs across seventeen states.

Beach projects received $10.9 million, about 23%. This funded ongoing sand placement at Pensacola Beach and Casino Beach parking improvements. The TDC's own 2023 strategic plan identified beach renourishment as the "single most critical infrastructure investment" for sustaining tourism. The spending ratio suggests other priorities.

Administrative costs—staff salaries, office operations, legal fees, consultants—totaled $3.1 million. That's 6.6% of collections, up from 4.8% five years ago. The TDC added two full-time positions in 2024 and hired an outside firm to conduct a $180,000 "brand perception study."

Capital reserves absorbed $8.7 million. Sports tourism grants took $2.9 million. The remainder scattered across smaller line items: $400,000 for a wayfinding sign program that has yet to install its first sign, $175,000 for an influencer partnership program, $89,000 for what meeting minutes describe as "industry relationship cultivation."

Measuring success, or not

Visit Pensacola, the county's destination marketing organization, presents monthly reports to the TDC. The metrics are consistent: website visits, social media impressions, advertising reach, email open rates.

What's missing is harder to track but arguably more important. The reports do not include return-on-investment calculations for specific campaigns. They do not compare Escambia County's tourism growth to competing Gulf Coast destinations. They do not measure whether advertising dollars in Chicago or Atlanta actually translate to heads in beds.

"We track what we can track," Visit Pensacola President Dana Young said at the April TDC meeting when a council member asked about conversion metrics. "The visitor journey is complex."

The complexity argument has limits. Destinations like Gulf Shores, Alabama, and Panama City Beach use third-party analytics firms to measure advertising effectiveness. Both publish annual economic impact reports with methodology sections. Escambia County's last such report was completed in 2021.

Young did not respond to emailed questions from The Flightline about Visit Pensacola's measurement practices.

The oversight gap

The TDC is advisory. It recommends. The Board of County Commissioners approves. In practice, the commissioners rarely alter TDC recommendations. Meeting records show the board has approved every TDC budget submission since 2018 without amendment.

Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, who serves as the board's TDC liaison, said commissioners trust the council's expertise.

"These are industry professionals," Bergosh said. "They understand tourism better than we do."

The industry professionals are, by design, industry participants. State law requires TDC membership to include hotel operators, attraction owners, and tourism business representatives. Seven of the council's nine voting members have financial interests in businesses that benefit from TDC-funded marketing.

This is not a conflict of interest under Florida law. It is the structure working as intended. But it creates a body that evaluates its own industry's requests for public money.

"The fox guarding the henhouse would be too strong," said Sarah Chen, a public administration professor at the University of West Florida who has studied Florida TDC structures. "But there's an inherent tension when beneficiaries control allocation."

The beach question

Pensacola Beach loses sand. Storms take it. Currents move it. The beach that draws 4.5 million visitors annually requires constant, expensive maintenance.

The Army Corps of Engineers estimates Escambia County needs $180 million in beach renourishment over the next decade to maintain current conditions. Federal cost-sharing typically covers 65%. The county's share: roughly $63 million.

At current allocation rates, beach funding from the TDC would total $109 million over ten years—if collections remain flat. But collections won't remain flat if the beach erodes. The circularity is obvious.

"You can't market a beach that isn't there," said Tom Wilkins, who owns three vacation rental properties on Via de Luna. Wilkins has attended TDC meetings for six years. He estimates he's spoken during public comment fifty times. "Every year I say the same thing. Every year they nod. Nothing changes."

TDC Chair Robert Morrison, who manages a Pensacola Beach resort, said the council balances competing needs.

"Beach funding is critical, absolutely," Morrison said. "But so is keeping Pensacola top-of-mind for travelers. If we stop marketing, they go to Destin. They go to Gulf Shores. We lose market share we might never get back."

The market share argument is difficult to verify. Florida does not publish destination-level tourism statistics. Visit Pensacola's claimed visitor counts come from internal models.

What transparency looks like

All TDC meetings are public. Agendas post three days in advance. Expenditure reports are available on the county website, if you know where to look. By the minimal requirements of Florida's public records law, the TDC is compliant.

By any more demanding standard, opacity persists.

Marketing contracts run to hundreds of pages. They are not posted online. A public records request for the current Visit Florida advertising contract took seventeen days to fulfill. The contract includes performance benchmarks, but the benchmarks are impressions and reach—the same metrics Visit Pensacola already reports, not independent verification of outcomes.

The Flightline requested five years of TDC member financial disclosure forms. The county responded that TDC members, as advisory board participants rather than county employees, are not required to file such disclosures.

Chen, the UWF professor, said this gap is common in Florida's TDC structure.

"Advisory boards exist in a gray zone," she said. "They have real influence over real money, but they don't have the disclosure requirements of elected officials or senior staff."

The path forward

The TDC's FY 2027 budget process begins next month. Staff projections anticipate $49 million in collections. The preliminary allocation framework, shared at May's meeting, proposes increasing marketing to 44% of expenditures.

Beach projects would remain at 23%.

Morrison said the council welcomes public input.

"We're here every second Tuesday," he said. "The meetings are open. People are welcome to come tell us what they think."

On Via de Luna, Wilkins is planning to be there again.

"Fifty-one times," he said. "Maybe fifty-one is the charm."

articles.label: Housing
articles.headline: The last trailer parks of Pensacola Beach
articles.dek: Decades-old mobile home communities on Santa Rosa Island face lease expirations and redevelopment pressure. For longtime residents, the clock is running out.
brief: Three mobile home communities on Pensacola Beach operate on Santa Rosa Island Authority leases set to expire within the next decade
Rising land values and redevelopment interest have prompted questions about whether leases will be renewed or properties converted to higher-revenue uses
Longtime residents, some who have lived on the island for 40 years, face uncertain futures with few affordable housing alternatives in the area
articles.body:
The wind chimes on Dolores Henley's porch have been marking time for 37 years. She hung them the week she moved into Paradise Mobile Home Park, a few hundred feet from the sound, back when a spot on Pensacola Beach cost her $180 a month.

Now 74, she sits in a lawn chair under a carport that's survived four hurricanes. The lot rent is $875. The chimes still ring. But the lease her park operates under expires in 2031, and nobody will tell her what happens after.

"They say don't worry about it," Henley said. "But I'm old. I'm not stupid."

Island arithmetic

Pensacola Beach is not like other Florida beaches. The land belongs to Escambia County, held in public trust and managed by the Santa Rosa Island Authority. Nobody owns the dirt. Residents and businesses lease it, some for decades at a time.

Three mobile home communities remain on the island: Paradise, Gulf Beach, and Sabine. Combined, they hold roughly 180 units. Their leases, negotiated in the 1990s, run on staggered timelines. All three expire before 2035.

SRIA Executive Director Paolo Ghio confirmed the lease terms but declined to discuss renewal prospects.

"Those conversations will happen at the appropriate time, with the appropriate parties," Ghio said in an email. "The Authority has no predetermined position."

The appropriate parties, in this case, are the park operators—not the residents. Mobile home owners lease their lots from the parks, which in turn lease the land from SRIA. It's a chain of tenancy that leaves the people at the bottom with the least leverage and the most to lose.

The math that matters

A single-family lot on Pensacola Beach generates roughly $12,000 to $15,000 per year in lease fees to SRIA. A comparable parcel developed as condominiums or a boutique hotel could generate three to five times that amount, according to a 2024 Authority financial analysis.

The three mobile home parks sit on some of the last underdeveloped acreage between Portofino and the toll plaza. Combined, they occupy nearly 22 acres of sound-front and interior lots.

"It's not hard to see where this goes," said Tom Reddick, a real estate attorney in Gulf Breeze who has represented mobile home owners in lease disputes across Florida. "The island has finite land. The pressure to maximize revenue from every parcel is enormous. Mobile homes don't pencil out anymore."

Escambia County's tourist development office reported $1.2 billion in visitor spending in the Pensacola Beach area in 2025. The beach's 4,500 permanent residents are outnumbered roughly 40 to 1 by annual visitors.

What 40 years buys you

At Gulf Beach Mobile Home Park, off Via de Luna, a hand-painted sign near the entrance reads "Family Community Since 1962." The units range from vintage Airstreams to double-wides with screened porches and satellite dishes. A communal dock juts into the sound. Children's bicycles lean against a storage shed.

Roy and Patsy Davenport moved to Gulf Beach in 1986. Roy was a Navy electrician at NAS Pensacola. Patsy worked at the Front Porch restaurant. They raised two kids in a 1,200-square-foot mobile home with a view of the sound.

"We weren't rich," Patsy said. "We were beach people. That used to be enough."

Their home, purchased outright 30 years ago, is worth approximately $45,000 according to a recent appraisal. Their lot lease runs $925 per month. If the park closes, they could theoretically move the structure—but relocation costs for a mobile home of that age typically run $15,000 to $25,000. And there's nowhere on the island to put it.

"We'd have to move to the mainland," Roy said. "At 71 years old. Start over."

The nearest mobile home parks accepting units are in Beulah, more than 20 miles north.

The silence from the Authority

The Flightline filed public records requests with SRIA for any communications regarding the mobile home park leases, renewal discussions, or expressions of interest from developers. The Authority provided 14 pages of documents, most of them routine lease payment records.

One email, from March 2025, referenced a "preliminary inquiry" from an unnamed development group regarding "potential future use" of the Paradise site. The inquiry was forwarded to Ghio with no documented response.

Board meeting minutes from the past three years contain no discussion of mobile home lease renewals.

SRIA board chair Tamara Fountain did not respond to interview requests. Two other board members declined to comment, citing pending lease negotiations.

"Pending with who?" asked Henley, the Paradise resident, when told of their response. "Nobody's negotiating with us."

The legal landscape

Florida's Mobile Home Act provides some protections for park residents, including notice requirements for rent increases and park closures. But those protections assume the park continues to operate. When a ground lease expires, the statute offers little remedy.

"The law protects you from your landlord," Reddick said. "It doesn't protect you from your landlord's landlord."

In 2019, residents of a mobile home park in Panama City Beach faced a similar situation when their park's lease expired and the landowner sold to a hotel developer. Residents received 180 days' notice. Some homes were moved. Most were demolished. A Marriott now occupies the site.

The Pensacola Beach leases contain clauses requiring "reasonable accommodation" for existing tenants in the event of non-renewal, but the term is undefined. Attorneys familiar with SRIA leases said the language has never been tested in court.

The people who stay

Not everyone at the parks is a retiree. At Sabine Mobile Home Park, the smallest of the three, a 34-year-old bartender named Chris Muñoz rents a lot for his Airstream. He works at a Pensacola Beach bar and surfs before his shifts.

"I know it's not permanent," Muñoz said. "Nothing out here is. But try finding a place on this beach for under a thousand a month. This is it."

His lease, passed through from the park to individual tenants, runs month to month. He could be gone in 30 days with proper notice.

"I think about it," he said. "Then I go look at the water and I stop thinking about it."

Down the row, a woman in her sixties was pressure-washing a deck. She declined to give her name. Asked about the lease situation, she shrugged.

"We've been hearing about this for 10 years," she said. "Developers, condos, the Authority, all of it. We're still here."

She turned the pressure washer back on. The conversation was over.

What comes next

SRIA's next public meeting is July 9. The agenda has not been posted. No mobile home lease discussions are expected, according to Authority staff.

Henley, the Paradise resident, said she plans to attend anyway. She's been going to meetings since 2018, sitting in the back, listening. She's never spoken during public comment.

"I keep thinking I'll know what to say," she said. "But what do you say? Please let me stay in my home? They know that already."

Her wind chimes caught a gust from the sound. She watched them swing.

"Thirty-seven years," she said. "I thought that would count for something."

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's new flight pattern brings noise complaints to Ferry Pass
articles.dek: Training route changes implemented this spring have shifted jet noise north. Residents want answers from a base that says it's following protocol.
brief: NAS Pensacola modified T-6 Texan II training patterns in March, shifting some flight paths over Ferry Pass neighborhoods
Escambia County has received over 200 noise complaints since April, a fivefold increase from the same period last year
Base officials cite safety protocols and airspace coordination but have not committed to a public meeting with affected residents
articles.body:
The jets come low over Doris Jenkins' backyard now. Four times a day, sometimes five. The orange and white T-6 Texan IIs bank hard over the tree line behind her house on Dorian Drive, close enough that she can see the silhouettes of student pilots in their cockpits.

"I've lived here 23 years," Jenkins said. "We always heard the base. That's part of living here. But this is different. This is in my living room."

Jenkins is one of more than 200 Escambia County residents who have filed formal noise complaints since April, when Naval Air Station Pensacola's modified training patterns became the new normal over Ferry Pass. The county's 311 system logged 41 noise complaints related to military aircraft in the same period last year.

The change traces back to March, when NAS Pensacola adjusted flight routes for Training Air Wing Six, which operates the T-6 Texan II turboprops used in primary flight training. Base officials confirmed the modification in a statement to The Flightline but declined to specify what prompted it.

"Training flight patterns are periodically adjusted to optimize safety, efficiency and coordination with FAA airspace requirements," the statement read. "NAS Pensacola remains committed to being a good neighbor while executing our primary mission of training the next generation of Naval and Marine Corps aviators."

The statement did not address whether the base had conducted any community outreach before implementing the changes.

A neighborhood unprepared

Ferry Pass sits roughly six miles north of the base's main runway. For decades, most training flights tracked over less populated areas to the west and south, looping over Perdido Bay or the industrial zones near the port. Residents north of the base heard aircraft but rarely felt them overhead.

That geography has shifted. Flight tracking data reviewed by The Flightline shows a marked increase in northbound departures and approach patterns over the Ferry Pass corridor since mid-March. On a typical training day, between 15 and 20 T-6 aircraft pass over the neighborhood during morning and afternoon sessions.

The T-6 Texan II is not a jet. Its Pratt & Whitney turboprop engine produces roughly 1,100 horsepower. But it's loud. At full power during climb-out, the aircraft generates noise levels comparable to a commercial airliner at similar altitude. The planes often pass over Ferry Pass at 1,500 to 2,000 feet—high enough to be legal, low enough to rattle windows.

Mike Underwood moved to a house on Dorian Circle eight months ago. He chose the neighborhood for its quiet streets and mature oak canopy. His real estate agent never mentioned the base.

"I'm not an anti-military guy. My dad was Navy," Underwood said. "But somebody should have told us this was coming. We would have at least known what we were signing up for."

County caught in the middle

Escambia County Commissioner Steven Barry, whose District 5 includes Ferry Pass, said his office has been inundated with calls and emails since April. He's asked the Navy for a public meeting. So far, no commitment.

"I understand the base has a mission. I respect that mission," Barry said. "But these are my constituents. They deserve to hear directly from the base about what changed and why."

Barry said he's requested data on the flight pattern modifications through the county's military affairs liaison. The Navy has not yet provided it.

Federal law gives military installations wide latitude over their airspace. NAS Pensacola coordinates with the FAA but is not required to notify local governments before adjusting training routes. The base operates under its own air traffic control and sets its own pattern altitude minimums, provided they meet Navy safety standards.

That regulatory structure leaves residents with few options. Noise complaints filed with the county get logged and forwarded to the base's community relations office. The base acknowledges receipt. Nothing changes.

No formal process

Unlike commercial airports, military installations in Florida are not subject to state noise mitigation requirements. NAS Pensacola has an Air Installations Compatible Use Zones study—a document that maps noise contours and recommends land use guidelines—but it was last updated in 2019. The current flight patterns do not match the contours in that study.

Jenkins said she tried calling the base directly. She got a voicemail. No one called back.

"I'm 67 years old. I'm not trying to shut down the Navy," she said. "I just want someone to explain why they're flying over my house now when they never did before. That doesn't seem like too much to ask."

The base's statement indicated that flight operations would continue as scheduled. Training Air Wing Six is currently in a high-tempo period ahead of summer graduations, with increased sortie rates expected through July.

Commissioner Barry said he would continue pressing for a public meeting. He did not sound optimistic.

"The base operates on its own timeline," he said. "We'll keep asking."
